rv.q: This play is as excruciatingly wrought as an episode of Fawlty Towers.
The Truth is joyous summer fun.
It’s definitely a comedy, and a very funny one at that.
Here, as ever, he serves the text without flash or fancy, and the result is a sleek night’s entertainment, full of explosive laughs.
This cocktail of evasions, delusions and selfishness slips down with delicious ease.

He also shares an obsession – artifice – and a style: quick, witty farce, so quick, indeed, it can hoist a hypocrite faster than his own petard. Michel (Stephen Mangan) is a cheat who comes to feel himself cheated. Who knows what to believe when the truth is a fickle mistress?
The psychological asides may be quintessentially French, but they’re not particularly profound.
But the truth is, the play is neither funny nor incisive enough to really grip.
The Truth is the most enjoyable comedy you may ever see in your entire life.
This is a hilarious comedy, and that’s the truth.
A winding, precisely plotted script, with philosophical overtones, is laugh-out-loud funny.
I’d advise audiences to go along for the gorgeously acted ride and save until later any nagging questions that may arise.
It offers a theatrical game rather than intellectual inquiry, and director Lindsay Posner serves it up accordingly as a satisfyingly funny entertainment for grown-ups.
Watching Mangan attempt to unfrazzle himself, is an absolute joy.

Instead, that all comes from the dialogue, in particular the increasing mania of Mangan as he struggles to stay in control of the web of lies. The trouble with relying on verbal comedy is that it relies upon the dialogue being whipcrack smart, and very often Zeller and Hampton fail to match that.
Yes, you can admire the smarts of the plotting, the technically perfect stagecraft and the comic timing, but, Gee, it’s hard to love.
This production is easily a hit, and that’s the truth!
Mangan is riveting in the demanding central role of Michel.
With plenty of laugh-out-loud moments, a touch of second-hand embarrassment and some absolutely fabulous acting, this is a great way to spend an evening.

A central conviction, which to some extent they all share, is that to hide wounding truths is actually altruistic. There’s are wonderful confrontations with his wife – Janie Dee a calm, adult Laurence – and with Paul (Ardal O”Hanlon, his deadpan quite remarkable).

Stephen Mangan who holds the whole thing together, carrying the audience through Michel's increasingly desperate house of cards with a performance that is career-defining: charming and in command of every beat.
The truth is, that The Truth is entertainment gold – an excellent script, a strong ensemble cast, and it is laugh-out-loud hilarious.

cn.t: Zeller's clever farce about infidelity earns mostly positive reviews for its intricate plotting and strong cast led by Mangan. Critics praise the witty dialogue and farcical complications, though some find it overly mannered or slight.
